FOR CLAT 2027
7

SC (No. of Judges) Amendment Bill, 2026


• On May 5, 2026, the Union Cabinet approved the Supreme Court
  (Number of Judges) Amendment Bill, 2026, which seeks to
  raise the apex court’s sanctioned strength.

• The Bill proposes to amend the Supreme Court (Number of
  Judges) Act, 1956, increasing the number of puisne judges from
  34 to 38 (including CJI).

• The move comes ahead of the Monsoon Session of Parliament, where
  the Bill is expected to be tabled for passage.

SC (No. of Judges) Amendment Bill, 2026

Constitutional Provisions –

• Article 124(1) of the Constitution originally provided that the
  Supreme Court shall consist of a Chief Justice of India and not more
  than seven other judges, unless Parliament by law prescribed a
  larger number.

• Unlike High Courts (Article 216, where the President can adjust judge
  strength through an executive order), the sanctioned strength of
  the Supreme Court can be changed only through an Act of
  Parliament.

• Every increase in SC judge strength has required amending the
  Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Act, 1956.

SC (No. of Judges) Amendment Bill, 2026


• Under Article 124(2), every judge of the Supreme Court is
  appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal, after
  consultation with such judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts
  as the President may deem necessary.

• Through judicial interpretation, the word “consultation” has come
  to mean concurrence of the Chief Justice of India, forming the basis
  of the collegium system of judicial appointments.

• Article 124(2A) of the Constitution fixes the retirement age of a
  Supreme Court judge at 65 years.

SC (No. of Judges) Amendment Bill, 2026


• Article 124(3) prescribes the eligibility criteria for appointment as a
  judge of the Supreme Court — a person must be:-

➢ (a) a citizen of India; and

➢ (b) either

    i.   a distinguished jurist in the opinion of the President,

    ii. a judge of one or more High Courts for at least five years, or

    iii. an advocate of a High Court for at least ten years.

SC (No. of Judges) Amendment Bill, 2026

Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Act, 1956 –

• It operationalizes Article 124(1) by fixing the exact number of
  puisne judges in the apex court, excluding the CJI.

• The 1956 Act originally set the strength at 10 judges (excluding
  the CJI).

• The Constitution does not prescribe a fixed number of judges beyond
  the initial “not more than seven” - Article 124(1); it expressly
  delegates to Parliament the power to increase the number by
  ordinary law.

SC (No. of Judges) Amendment Bill, 2026



• The strength of the Supreme Court was raised to 14 (including CJI)
  in 1960, and further increased to 18 (including CJI) in 1977.

• In 1986, the sanctioned strength was increased to 26 (including
  CJI), responding to a sharp rise in litigation after the Emergency.

• The judge strength was increased to 31 (including CJI) in 2008-09,
  through amendments to the 1956 Act.

SC (No. of Judges) Amendment Bill, 2026



• The salaries, allowances and pensions of Supreme Court judges
  are “charged” upon the Consolidated Fund of India under Article
  112(3)(d) of the Constitution, read with the Supreme Court
  (Number of Judges) Act, 1956.

• As a charged expenditure, this amount is non-votable and is not
  subject to the annual approval of the Lok Sabha.

SC (No. of Judges) Amendment Bill, 2026


• In its 229th Report (2009), the 18th Law Commission (chaired
  by Justice A.R. Lakshmanan) took a fundamentally different
  approach from simply adding more judges.

• The Commission recommended dividing the Supreme Court into
  four Cassation (Regional) benches at -

➢ Northern Region: New Delhi

➢ Southern Region: Chennai or Hyderabad

➢ Eastern Region: Kolkata

➢ Western Region: Mumbai

SC (No. of Judges) Amendment Bill, 2026


• Despite being formally forwarded to the government, the 229th
  Report has never been implemented.

• A writ petition filed in 2016 has been pending before the
  Supreme Court, seeking the establishment of a National Court of
  Appeal (NCA), which would act as an intermediate appellate forum
  between High Courts and the Supreme Court.

• The concept of NCA has been floated since the Bihar Legal
  Support Society case (1985) and was revived by the 229th Law
  Commission Report.

SC (No. of Judges) Amendment Bill, 2026


Procedure to Increase Seats –

• The Chief Justice of India sends a proposal to the Union Ministry
  of Law and Justice, citing workload and pendency as the basis for
  increasing judge strength.

• The Law Ministry, after consulting the Finance Ministry, prepares a
  draft amending Bill and places it before the Union Cabinet for
  approval.

• Once the Cabinet approves, the Supreme Court (Number of
  Judges) Amendment Bill is introduced in Parliament.

SC (No. of Judges) Amendment Bill, 2026


• Amending the 1956 Act does not require a constitutional
  amendment; the Bill needs only a simple majority in both Houses
  of Parliament.

• Article 368 is not triggered, so no special majority (two-thirds)
  or state ratification is needed, making the process faster.

• After passage, the Bill goes to the President for assent; once given,
  the Act comes into force, and the President can appoint additional
  judges up to the new limit on the Collegium’s advice.

SC (No. of Judges) Amendment Bill, 2026

The Three Judges Case –

• First Judges Case (1981) – S.P. Gupta v. Union of India, a
  Seven-judge Bench held that “consultation” with the CJI under
  Article 124(2) did not mean “concurrence”, and the President could
  override the CJI’s advice for “cogent reasons”.

• The ruling gave the executive the final say in judicial
  appointments, reiterating that the President – acting on the aid and
  advice of the Council of Ministers – was the ultimate appointing
  authority.

• The judgment is also known for its clarification on locus standi in
  public interest litigation (PIL).

SC (No. of Judges) Amendment Bill, 2026


• Second Judges Case (1993) – A nine-judge Bench in Supreme
  Court Advocates-on-Record Association v. Union of India
  overruled the First Judges Case and held that “consultation” under
  Article 124(2) must be interpreted as “concurrence”.

• The SC established the Collegium System, defining its composition as
  the Chief Justice of India (CJI) and the two senior-most
  judges of the Supreme Court.

• Justices A.M. Ahmadi and M.M. Punchhi dissented, warning that
  such a fundamental change required a constitutional amendment, not
  a judicial one.

SC (No. of Judges) Amendment Bill, 2026


• Third Judges Case (1998) – On a Presidential Reference (Article
  143), a nine-judge Bench in In re Special Reference 1 of
  1998 expanded the Collegium to its present composition: the CJI
  and the four senior-most judges of the Supreme Court.

• The court ruled that Collegium decisions must be based on
  “consensus” rather than majority, with opinions recorded in writing
  and all relevant material placed on record for transparency.

• The ruling clarified that “consultation” under Article 124(2)
  necessarily meant “concurrence” of the Collegium, consolidating the
  judicial appointments system that the NJAC later tried (and failed) to
  replace.

SC (No. of Judges) Amendment Bill, 2026

NJAC Act (2014) –

• Parliament passed the 99th Constitutional Amendment Act and
  the National Judicial Appointments Commission Act, 2014 to
  replace the Collegium with a six-member Commission.

• The NJAC comprised the CJI, two senior-most SC judges, the Union
  Law Minister, and two “eminent persons” nominated by a committee
  of the PM, CJI and Leader of Opposition.

• The NJAC could veto any recommendation if at least two of its
  members disagreed, introducing executive and civil-society oversight
  into the appointments process.

•

SC (No. of Judges) Amendment Bill, 2026


• A five-judge Constitution Bench, by a 4:1 majority on October 16,
  2015, declared both the 99th Amendment and the NJAC Act
  unconstitutional.

• The court held that non-judicial members (including the Law
  Minister) could veto the judiciary’s nominees,
  endangering judicial independence.

• The verdict made the Collegium the sole valid mechanism for
  appointing higher judiciary judges, making India the only
  constitutional democracy where judges select judges without any
  executive or parliamentary role.

SC (No. of Judges) Amendment Bill, 2026


Recent News –

• The most recent revision before the 2026 Bill came in 2019, when
  Parliament increased the number of judges from 31 to 34 including
  the CJI.

• That increase was recommended by then CJI Ranjan Gogoi, who
  had flagged rising pendency as a major concern.

• Even before the 2026 expansion was proposed, the working strength
  of the Supreme Court was 34-2 = 32 judges as of early 2026,
  because there were two vacancies against the sanctioned
  strength of 34.

SC (No. of Judges) Amendment Bill, 2026


• Chief Justice of India Surya Kant has publicly welcomed the
  government’s decision to raise the SC judge strength to 38

• He stated that the move will help address case pendency and ensure
  faster disposal of Constitution Bench matters. His tenure runs
  till February 2027.

• The Cabinet’s approval to increase SC judges to 38 responds to
  over 92,000 pending cases, but does not address deeper
  institutional reforms in appointment and listing practices.

India’s New CDS



• The Government of India has appointed Lieutenant General N S
  Raja Subramani (Retd) as the country’s next Chief of defence
  Staff (CDS).

• He will also serve as Secretary, Department of Military Affairs
  (DMA) in the Ministry of defence.

• Lt Gen Raja Subramani will assume office after the incumbent CDS
  General Anil Chauhan completes his term on 30th May 2026.

India’s New CDS

Background –

• The Kargil Review Committee (KRC) , headed by Shri K.
  Subrahmanyam, after the 1999 conflict first recommended
  structural reforms in India’s higher defence management.

• The KRC highlighted the lack of a single-point military adviser and
  the need for integration among the three services at the highest
  level.

• Its report formed the basis for the government’s subsequent efforts
  to create the CDS post.

India’s New CDS


• Based on the KRC report, the Cabinet Committee on Security
  appointed a Group of Ministers (GoM) in 2000 headed by then
  Deputy Prime Minister L K Advani to recommend defence
  reforms.

• The GoM submitted 75 recommendations, including the creation
  of a Chief of defence Staff to function as a single-point military
  adviser.

• However, eight recommendations – including the CDS proposal –
  remained under consideration for nearly two decades.

India’s New CDS


• In 2012, the government appointed a Task Force headed by
  former Cabinet Secretary Naresh Chandra to assess the
  implementation of earlier defence reform recommendations.

• The Naresh Chandra Task Force reportedly recommended the
  appointment of a permanent Chairman of the Chiefs of Staff
  Committee (a four-star officer) rather than a five-star CDS.

• Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced the creation of the CDS as
  a four-star officer in 2019.

India’s New CDS


• The DMA was created as a fifth department within the Ministry
  of defence , alongside the Department of defence , defence
  Production, defence R&D and Ex-Servicemen Welfare.

• General Bipin Rawat, then Chief of the Army Staff, was appointed
  as India’s first CDS on 31st December 2019.

• Tragically, General Rawat died in a helicopter crash on
  8th December 2021, after which General Anil Chauhan was
  appointed as the second CDS.

India’s New CDS


• The CDS has two roles: (1) Permanent Chairman of the Chiefs
  of Staff Committee (military role) and (2) Secretary,
  Department of Military Affairs (government role).

• He serves as the Principal Military Adviser to the defence
  Minister on tri-services matters, but the service chiefs continue to
  advise on matters concerning their respective services.

• The CDS does not exercise any military command over the
  three service chiefs, but enjoys significant influence because the
  DMA oversees personnel matters of the three services.

India’s New CDS


• The CDS holds the rank of a four-star officer – equivalent to the
  Chief of the Army Staff, Chief of the Naval Staff and Chief of the Air
  Staff.

• Domestically, the CDS ranks 12th in the Indian order of
  precedence – the same as the three service chiefs.

• He is also the status-equivalent of the service chiefs in terms of
  protocol and entitlements.

India’s New CDS


• As per current rules, the CDS serves till attaining the age of 65
  years.

• The government can appoint a retired three-star officer
  (Lieutenant General level equivalent) or a retired service chief
  to the post, as long as the officer is below 62 years of age.

• Subramani is the third CDS from the Army, following General Bipin
  Rawat (2020-21) and General Anil Chauhan (2022-26).

India’s New CDS


• The CDS draws a basic salary of ₹2.5 lakh per month, which is
  the same as that of the three service chiefs (Apex Scale, Level 18 of
  the 7th CPC).

• In addition to salary, the CDS is entitled to all the perquisites and
  allowances of a Secretary to the Government of India.

• The CDS also receives the same pension and retirement
  benefits as the service chiefs.

India’s New CDS


• The President is the Supreme Commander of the Indian Armed
  Forces.

• The Ministry of Defence (MoD) acts as the executive agency for
  defence matters, headed by the Defence Minister who is responsible
  to Parliament for all defence matters.

•    Under Article 246 read with Union List – Entry 1, Parliament
    has exclusive legislative control over “Defence of India” and the
    Armed Forces.

India’s New CDS

• The National Security Council (NSC) is the apex body for
  formulating India’s national security policies. It was established in
  1998 with a three-tier structure:

➢ Strategic Policy Group (SPG)

➢ National Security Advisory Board (NSAB)

➢ National Security Council Secretariat (NSCS).

• The NSC is chaired by the Prime Minister, with the National
  Security Adviser serving as its Secretary and coordinator.

India’s New CDS


• According to the Global Firepower Index 2025, India’s military is
  ranked the fourth most powerful in the world (after the United
  States, Russia, and China).

• India’s defence budget for 2025-26 was ₹6.81 lakh crore,
  with ₹1.86 lakh crore allocated for capital modernisation,
  and ₹7.84 lakh crore for 2026-27.

•

India’s New CDS


Theaterisation –

• Theaterisation seeks to integrate the Army, Navy, Air Force and
  their resources into specific ‘theatre’ commands, for deployment
  under a single, unified command structure in a given
  geographical region.

• Currently, the Army and IAF have seven commands each, and the
  Navy has three, with only two tri-service commands (Andaman &
  Nicobar and Strategic Forces Command).

• The reform aims to ensure jointness, reduce duplication of
  assets, and improve combat effectiveness in a multi-domain conflict.

India’s New CDS


• The military has finalized a three-command structure:

➢ Pakistan-focused Western Theatre (to be headed by an IAF
  officer),

➢ China-focused Northern Theatre (headed by an Army officer)
  and

➢ Maritime Theatre (headed by a Navy officer).

India’s New CDS


• The Western Theatre will be headquartered in Jaipur, the Northern
  Theatre in Lucknow, and the Maritime Theatre
  in Thiruvananthapuram.

• More than 90 per cent of the planning for theatre commands has
  been completed.

• The government expects to operationalise the first theatre
  command by May 2026, serving as a template for full transition
  over the next two years.

India’s New CDS

Recent News –

• N S Raja Subramani has four decades of distinguished
  service, currently serving as Military Adviser at the National
  Security Council Secretariat (NSCS).

• Subramani previously served as Vice Chief of the Army
  Staff (July 2024 – July 2025) and General Officer
  Commanding-in-Chief, Central Command (March 2023 –
  June 2024).

• Known within the military circles as a “soldier-scholar”, he holds
  an MA from King’s College London and an M.Phil in defence
  Studies from Madras University.

India’s New CDS


• Alongside the CDS, the government has appointed Vice Admiral
  Krishna Swaminathan as the next Chief of the Naval Staff.

• Swaminathan, who is heading the Mumbai-based Western Naval
  Command, will take charge on 31st May 2026, succeeding Admiral
  Dinesh K Tripathi.

• Swaminathan is a specialist in communication and electronic warfare
  and an alumnus of the National defence Academy,
  Khadakvasla, Maharashtra.
